utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I believe that both parties have received that proofing notes for the next witness furnished by the Prosecution, the affidavit submitted by the OTP investigator as well as the reports from the VWU units. So, Mr. Morrissey, do you have anything to say at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have been given those reports. I'm going to cross-examine this witness on them. I don't seek to revisit Your Honours' ruling at this stage. It seems that they -- what would -- the issue would be overtaken by events in any event. But, Your Honour, what I want to put on record is this: The Prosecutor forces the hand of this Tribunal when it makes late applications. The Tribunal is not in a position to -- to dismiss lightly allegations that somebody is under threat and you don't want to take a risk with a witness in case that threat proves to be true. When the Prosecutor makes a practice, and it plainly is a practice of doing this late, it increases the danger of there being a secret trial because you, the Tribunal, must be -- must err on the side of caution. You have to do so. And it just places the Defence in an impossible TO position to do this if they do it at a late stage. The pattern in this trial is all too clear. It's a policy. It cannot be said to be late. The material that you've got before you now makes it clear. This application could and should have been made two weeks ago. Whatever the reasons may be, Your Honour, I'm not proposing to ask you to revisit your ruling. I'm just going to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation, and I believe one point you said is -- is pretty valued, that is, that if the party calling the witness asking for some protective measures, they have to make it as early as possible. So the rulings we made concerning of the protective measures for the next witness remained unchanged. And could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I would like to give the witness the -- his pseudonym sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Do you see a piece of paper before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is your name, date of birth, and the place you were born reflected on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May I please now tender this under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe the there's no objections from the Defence. Yes, it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Obliged, Your Honour. Now, with the Court's permission, I will lead the witness on his personal particulars.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet will be Prosecution Exhibit P183, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before the war, you lived in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You worked as a waiter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You graduated from secondary school and studied catering for four years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: From 1987 to 1988, you served in the JNA, which is the Yugoslav People's Army, as a cook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On 6th April 1992, you joined the TO in the Stari Grad municipality in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were in a group of about 30 people who were mostly neighbours and you guarded the families and patrolled the streets of the city.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In May 1992, you became a member of the 1st Sandzak Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the commander of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Merdzo Haznadar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you please, please, Witness, at the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993, what did you do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In late 1993 and early -- late 1992-1993, we left the Sandzak Brigade and declared ourselves the military police unit in the school in Bratina, where Ramiz Delalic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was the name of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: This was a unit of the military police. The military police. And later on, a brigade was made up of this military police and the name of it was the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you said the commander was Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. Ramiz Delalic was the deputy brigade commander, and Suljo Imsirovic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were you in any particular unit of this 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was in the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in this assault detachment in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: About 50 to 60 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what is the function and purpose of an assault unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: To go out for combat activities. So it was not to be in trenches and to keep the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How well equipped were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: What do you mean how well equipped were we? As a unit, we were armed quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What kind of arms were you bearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: RPGs, hand-held launchers, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what were you doing in September 1993, your -- this unit, this brigade that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In September, on the 7th of September, this unit at the headquarters of our brigade in Trampina Street received an order from the Supreme Command with Mr. Sefer Halilovic at its head that we were to go to deblock Mostar in the Neretva offensive. On that day, we received that order and we set out sometime in the afternoon in small cars as far as the tunnel. Then we went through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Witness. I'd like to take you through slowly, if I may, please. Can you tell us when you received this order, what do you mean "we received this order"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Our brigade received an order from the Supreme Command, from the Supreme Command of the staff. Mr. Sefer Halilovic was at its head. We received an order from Mr. Sefer Halilovic in writing, and it's now in the possession of a person in Sarajevo who will certainly come to testify here. And we had to go and lift the siege of Mostar. This was the Neretva operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you about this order or did you all receive one individually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. In the brigade, they told us. They told us in the command, when they lined us up, before we were to set out. They said we had received this order, that we were to go to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who told you this? The name of the person, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Before we set out that day, a gentleman arrived. His name was Vahid Karavelic. He was the corps commander. He was the deputy commander. And Suljo Imsirovic, the brigade commander, and Delalic Ramiz, his deputy. And they read out this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Celo there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Ramiz Delalic was Celo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there assembled when you were told this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were 50 or 60 soldiers, but 25 or 30 of them were from our assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who were the rest from? Which other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: From our brigade but other battalions. All of them were from our brigade. Our brigade had 5.000 soldiers. I couldn't know them all personally. Some men were separated off who had been in the brigade, and the battalion commanders sent them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So all of them were from the 9th Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what exactly was said to you, to the assembled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They told us who were assembled there that we were to go to Herzegovina to lift the siege of Mostar, and on our arrival in Herzegovina we would learn the details. We were going to another area of responsibility, and our commander would no longer be commanding us there. It would be Zulfikar Alispago. We would be under his command. And the leader of this operation would be Commander Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was the name of this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were told this, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In whose zone of responsibility were you going in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was of the 4th or 6th Corps. I'm not sure. It was where those two corps joined up. Salko Gusic was the commander of the 6th Corps, and I think Mr. Drekovic was the commander of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Had you known Sefer Halilovic before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He used to come to our brigade, to our command, to our headquarters. He toured all the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He was the Chief of Staff. He wasn't the commander of the army, but he was the Chief of Staff because establishment-wise this duty was not yet established.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did he have any other function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell me what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: What do you mean? You mean when the brigade set off or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this was 7 September, you said. Did you set off on the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, on the same day in the evening, at around 7.00, we set out. Passing through Dobrinja was risky because there was shooting. So it was quite risky getting to the tunnel. When we set out, we set out in small cars, several soldiers in each car. We reached the tunnel, passed through the tunnel, arrived in Hrastici, where we were met by Mr. Fikret --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last name --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Who was to secure transport for us to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who else was travelling with you of the commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Only Ante Delalic [phoen] and the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Malco Rovcanin, Nihad Vlahovljak, Nevzet Sabanovic, the commander of my platoon, and a few others whose names escape me now. And the soldiers who were with us, if you want to know their names, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us the soldiers' names that you remember, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Nedzad Mihanovic, Erdin Arnautovic, Nevzet Sabanovic, Sulejman -- Pilica Samir, Jasmin Mendic [phoen], Hukelic Ertan, Malco Rovcanin, and several others.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you reach a certain village in the early hours of the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On the 8th of September, we arrived in Donja Jablanica, where Zulfikar Alispago's headquarters was, where this gentleman met us. It was around 7.00 or 8.00. We had breakfast and Zuka said they would put us up in this village called Grabovica. After breakfast, we got onto trucks from Hrasnica, and they put us up in the village of Grabovica, where there were Croatian civilians. On the right-hand side were Croatian civilians, and on the left-hand side were Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you pass a checkpoint where there -- something happened on the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd object to that. Your Honour will recall that this checkpoint has been attempted to be led by my learned friends Mr. Re and Mr. Weiner with different witnesses. It's entirely irrelevant to the charges. It doesn't go to any material fact at all. And I object to it as irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but I don't think so. I believe that the previous witness has already testified about that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It might -- there's -- it depends which checkpoint. Perhaps if my learned friend could make clear which one she's talking about. Your Honour will recall there's one I objected to and there's others which are clearly relevant. So if it's clarified which one we're talking about, I'll -- I'll see what I'll take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you go to any checkpoint as you travelled before you got to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I clarify. It will assist -- it will assist everyone in court, including my learned friend. I don't object to questioning about any checkpoint after Jablanica on the way to Grabovica. That's plainly relevant. It's that -- what happened en route between -- between Hrasnica and Jablanica which was the cause of controversy before. And perhaps if my friend could clarify which one she's talking about, then we'll know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please, please clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In the village of Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I do object. Your Honour, the evidence is -- well, it -- the map will show in any event that Pazaric lies between Hrasnica but before they arrive at Jablanica. So I object to it as irrelevant, as I did with the other two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What's -- what's the relevance of that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The relevance of that checkpoint, Your Honour, is that -- the behaviour of the soldiers, and that's directly relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe there's some follow-up questions on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we -- we will see how relevant it is. You may --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We're talking about a checkpoint. Did you -- did you encounter a checkpoint before you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Do you mean before or after Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before. Before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Before Jablanica, there was a checkpoint in Pazaric -- no, not Pazaric. What's the name of that place now? Where the road branches off from Igman when you reach the main road leading from Hadzici. That's where there was a checkpoint. There was some sort of military police there, some kind of police, and they stopped us. It was early in the morning, about 3.00 a.m. perhaps. And there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd ask the witness to stop there, please. Now, I maintain the objection here. Unless my learned friend says it's part of the Prosecutor's case that Sefer Halilovic was there and knew about this; otherwise, it's just a piece of irrelevant wayside journey, in my submission. It's not part of the Prosecution's case just to show what behaviour may have happened or may not have happened in the atmosphere. The question is whether Sefer Halilovic was there and knew about it. Now, if it's part of the Prosecution's case that he knew about the Pazaric crossroads, then my friend had better say so. Otherwise, it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, with due respect, it's directly part of the Prosecution case, the behaviour of these particular soldiers, and how they were behaving on their way. I cannot see whether Sefer Halilovic was there or not precludes us from calling such evidence. It's generally the mood of the soldiers as they -- as they went for this combat operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't think that that piece of the evidence is the most important one, but I believe that the evidence may be useful in the Defence case in the future, so we'll allow the questions to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what happened at this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First I have to say that this checkpoint existed from the beginning of the war. This was some kind of border toward Hadzici. So ever since the war broke out and Igman was liberated, there was a checkpoint there, and there was a minor incident at that checkpoint because there was some kind of disagreement between my fellow fighters and the soldiers manning the checkpoint. Perhaps they were drunk or they were nervous. They wouldn't let us through. And they asked for special passes. As in this period, soldiers of the army were fleeing Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who? Who was drunk and nervous?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, those soldiers at the checkpoint, who were manning the checkpoint and guarding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what kind of -- what ensued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There was some kind of conflict, and then they let us through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was -- was any weapons -- were any weapons fired off in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving right along. You went to Zuka's base, you said. And who did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Mr. Zuka came out. He had to take over our unit. We were now under his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who is Zuka? Do you know -- did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I knew Zuka from November 1992, when we went to Igman. There was supposed to be some sort of offensive on a village called Junavica [phoen]. There was some kind of military depots there with weapons. And the aggressors were there. I met Zuka there. We spent some 15 or 20 days there. We were unable to carry out this action and we returned to Sarajevo because of the snow.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was Zuka -- you told the Court earlier that Zuka was to be now your commander for this operation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you know who Zuka's commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was Salko Gusic or the commander of the 4th Corps, Drekovic. These two corps later were united. And from that day onward it was Mr. Sefer Halilovic who was in charge of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So he would be Zuka's commander, would he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours can see what the objection to that is. The witness has given evidence, A, my learned friend in a leading question has now tried to get him to say B. Now, it's impermissible in a number of ways and I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that question is a little bit leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was the -- the commander of the operation that you'd gone for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The main commander of the operation was Mr. Sefer Halilovic, that is, of Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you said you went to Grabovica. Can you tell me, when you went there, what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When we set out with trucks, nothing actually happened immediately. We reached this village and were given some blankets. We were received by the locals there, the civilians, who took us in as if we were they're own family. And that's how we spent the entire day, until the afternoon on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Other than the civilians -- and what ethnicity were these civilians from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The civilians we were put up with were of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who else did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were Muslim refugees in a house in this village. There were four of them, I believe. I can't say exactly. Or rather -- yes, I'm certain that there were four of them and they -- they were refugees and they were received by the local Croats there, who shared their home with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were there any other troops present when you arrived in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were Solakovic's 2nd Independent Battalion men. There were Cedo's Wolves, Zuka's troops, and a bit further on there were those from the Handzar Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And where did you find accommodation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was put up in an abandoned house that didn't have a roof at the time, nor does it still have one today. Some of the houses were reconstructed, but this one is still vacant. And at the time, it was abandoned. It was pretty much neglected.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness I'm going to show you --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And I'm going to show him P4, Your Honour. There'll be a photograph which will come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like him -- the witness to mark certain houses, Your Honour. So if I can have a copy presented to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, what I would like you now to do is put a circle around the house where you were accommodated and put a "1" on top of that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, Witness, who else was accommodated in this house with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In this particular house, there was me, Arnautovic Erdin, Malco Rovcanin, and Ramiz Delalic spent one night in the house. That was when the children fled the village prior to the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to look at this photograph again, if you would, please, and tell me the houses of the other -- some other soldiers that you know and units which were billeted. Can you locate us -- tell me what other houses that you recall and who was billeted in these houses? If you'd put -- give me the name first. Then you can circle it, and then put a "2".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In this house, the 2nd Independent Battalion was put up, Adnan Solakovic, who was the commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion. In this particular house, there were Hasid Basovic, Fikret Kraljevic, Hota Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Any other house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There was a house here, but you can't really see it now, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Number 4. That's where Sulejman Lujinovic was put up and a man by the name of Crni. I don't know his last name. And Nedzad Mehanovic, who actually went around the village. Mahovljak [phoen] slept in this particular house along with his fellow fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that the markings are quite clear. If we could make sure that the 1, 2, 3, 4 --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Any other house that you recognise there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There was another house here. That's where the engineers slept, members of the engineering unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And that would be 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: 6. And there were these houses where the local residents lived, civilians. And there was another house above the railway track.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And all these houses that you've marked, who -- who was residing in them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were Croats living in all these houses. They were the local residents there. Before that, there were JNA units that had liberated the village, but that was a couple of months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this, Your Honour. That would be ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P184.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what did you do that -- after you went into that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When I came to the house, all those who were with me - and I've enumerated them - who slept with me in the house, weren't there. I was alone. I was cleaning the house all day long so that we could have a place to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And after cleaning this house, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I went over to the house just across from my house - not below the road - where we had a coffee. I was there with the local residents and with my fellow fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And whose house was it that you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: A man lived in this house, an elderly man, who was suffering from this illness. I don't know how you call it, when you have the shakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who else was in that house, other than this old man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were those Muslim refugees, a man, his wife, and two children, who had -- who were some 12 or 13 years of age. Then there was Mustafa, Fikret Kraljevic, Nevzet Sabanovic. We were actually all of us there. We were sitting at a table having coffee and having a laugh.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do after -- what did you do at this house, other than sit around the table and have a laugh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Since we didn't have good quality food those days, the local resident offered some lamb or -- they actually gave us their sheep so that we could have something to eat that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then what did you do after you'd finished this barbecue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I went back to the house, where I continued cleaning because it was in a very bad state.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where did you sleep at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Erdin Arnautovic slept outdoors, because we spent more time outdoors than indoors. It was very dirty inside and the smell was terrible. All the other troops, soldiers, slept in the other houses, where they had a fair kind of accommodation, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you hear anything at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Nothing was happening during the night. There were no actions, murders, or crimes. The entire night between the 8th and the 9th September was a very peaceful one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened the next day? What did you do in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The next day, we woke, had a cup of coffee, sat together, talked, socialised, until midday, noon. At that point, Vehbija Karic, Sefer Halilovic, Zuka, and other commanders from the Supreme Command, who were there, came. They lined up all the units that were there and the units were lined up just in front of the house where I slept in, because there was a plain, a plateau there where everybody could be lined up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I just want to take you through this very slowly, if you -- if you please, Witness, would indulge me. You said Vehbija Karic, Sefer Halilovic, and Zuka came, and Ramiz Delalic. Is that your testimony? Are these the four people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He did not say Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I thought he had --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Ramiz Delalic there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. Just a moment. Your Honour, it's -- it's really basic to have to make this submission. I apologise for having to make it. But you can see I have to make it. Suggesting to the witness the answer that he should be giving by a leading question is a very grave evil in a case like this. It's not just a slip or a mistake. It can't be done. It can't be allowed. Your Honours, I don't wish to be objecting every 30 seconds to that sort of thing. It shouldn't happen, and I object to it. I don't know what else I can do except object on a case-by-case basis. But I ask Your Honour to have regard to what looks like a pattern of leading, and I do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana, we came to the most important part of evidence. So just be careful about the leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought he had said. I hadn't looked at transcript. Yes, I take on board what counsel's objection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Just be cautious.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Witness, who came, the names of all the people you saw were coming, one by one, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, Vehbija Karic, Zulfikar Alispago. Ramiz Delalic wasn't there because he came in afterwards when the children were found. I highlighted this because there were some difficulties with the gentleman I was giving a statement to, to this man Nikolai. I don't know what was going on there. Because he came on after all those murders and events had taken place. All those incidents in Grabovica took place outside his presence. He came only when those children were brought in. There were other commanders there who were sitting on a curb outside this house that I was sleeping in. They were seated on this curb. Sefer was seated on a small chair. The rest were sitting on this concrete slab or whatever or were squatted down. The commanders of the units called on all of their soldiers to show up. There were some 100 to 150 men there. And then there was talk about what this offensive was to look like. This was the Operation Neretva to lift the blockade of Mostar. Mr. Sefer Halilovic was the one speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, can I interrupt you? As I -- I'd like to take this slowly. And if you would be so kind as to answer my questions and all of this will come out in the fullness of time. Now, can you tell me which other commanders were there other than the three that you have mentioned. You said six other commanders. Who were they? Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There was Salko Gusic. And then there were Cedo's Wolves. I don't know what his name was. There was Handzar's Division. I don't know what the commander's name was. I don't know what their names were. I think that Cedo's Wolves were commanded by Mr. Sadic. I believe that was his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And had you known Vehbija Karic before you saw him that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I remember Vehbija Karic very well from the media prior to the outbreak of the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the cannons were positioned above Sarajevo, he was an artillery man. And then Vehbija Karic said when asked why the guns were positioned, he said, "Because of the Defence of the town." I know him from the town as the commander of the artillery there. Although, this was not much of an artillery, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Other than on the media, had you ever seen him before yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I used to see him in the different staffs when he would come to tour different units.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how did these people come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: These people were brought in in jeeps. And I mean to Grabovica. They were brought in in jeeps from the direction of Jablanica. I don't know where they set out from.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was driving the jeeps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Sefer's vehicle was driven by a man that I knew very well. His name was Mesko -- or rather, his nickname was Mesko. I don't know his real name. The other jeep was driven by Dino.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to show you P7, Witness. This is a photograph which you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before that's done. I wonder if my friend would like to clarify the identity of this person who's called Dino here. Because we have had a Dino who gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Edin Arnautovic, also known as Dino.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you look at the photograph, please, P7. Did you on that particular photograph circle where it was that this meeting that you say was held, where the commanders came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First of all, there -- this forest or this grove of trees wasn't there at the time. There was just this plain. The meeting of the commanders took place on this sidewalk or slab, right here. That's where all these commanders were seated. And the army was here, where I make the circle, where there are no trees. That's where Sefer, Vehbija Karic, Zuka, Gusic, and all the other commanders who were there were seated. Sefer was here, at this angle. When they arrived, they greeted all the soldiers, asked how they had been accommodated, and then started talking about the offensive Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I would like to first finish with the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can I please tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection, but I'm not sure if the copy I -- whether the witness put any numbers on -- the drawing stopped on our copy at a fairly early stage in the narrative. And I'm not sure. The witness seemed to be indicating something on the picture which hasn't appeared on ours. I'm just not sure that we've got the full -- the same thing that the Prosecutor has gone. I'm told by the court deputy that I've got what the Prosecutor has got. I have no objection to it being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Just to clarify, witness, the circle that you've drawn, is that where the meeting was held, or is there anywhere else that you want to identify on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I just want to specify that this grove of trees was not there at the time. These photographs were taken obviously in the late summer, when the trees are already full of leaves. There was just a plain there some 50 metres long and 10 metres wide where the entire troops were. I've circled the trees as -- marking it as an area where the troops were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite clear that, the trees weren't there, so there would be a plain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this one, if there's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like you to cast your mind back. And when these commanders came, who was there? When they first came, who was there in that area that you have just indicated to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That's where I, Nevzet Sabanovic, and some other soldiers were. We were sitting down and preparing lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So when they first came, how many soldiers were present, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were five or six of us. I can't recall all the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do when they first came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We were making lunch and there was a small cottage nearby where I took some honey from. We greeted all the commanders, shook hands with Sefer Halilovic and all the others, and they came and sat down on this slab of concrete outside this house. I offered them some honey and they took some. They had their own conversation waiting for the soldiers to gather.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then which soldiers came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: All the units that were there, Cedo's Wolves, the 2nd Independent Battalion, Handzar's Division, Zuka's men, and all the others. In all, there were 100 to 150 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please now tell us what happened after all these soldiers gathered. But before you do that, I would like to ask you -- no, in fact, you have actually answered that. Yes, can you tell us what exactly happened when all the soldiers congregated. Who spoke first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When all the soldiers assembled, Sefer Halilovic spoke first, as commander of the operation, and he made it quite clear to all of us, the soldiers there, that he was commander of the Operation Neretva, that this was to be a very difficult battle to lift the siege of Mostar, that it was going to last for who knows how long, and that we would not return until Mostar had been liberated at any cost, so that we were going to stay there until we basically capture Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the reaction of the soldiers to this speech of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The soldiers were silent. They were being addressed by the commander of the army, the person in charge of the operation. So they listened to him in silence. There might have been some commotion, but nobody made any comments in relation to that. The soldiers held him in high esteem and nobody commented on it

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened? Who was the next to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Mr. Vehbija Karic was the next one to speak. He was seated next to Sefer. When they had finished explaining the operation and told us that we were to leave the following evening, then Vehbija Karic enquired after our accommodation, whether everything was in order in the village, and a soldier spoke out and said that not everything was going well, that they had some criticism to level at the civilians there, and that's where Vehbija Karic -- when Vehbija Karic said, "Well, then just let's execute them or summarily throw them into the river."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like you to really go back on this and try to recall, if you will, the exact words spoken by Vehbija Karic, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Vehbija Karic's words were, "Under summary procedure, throw them all into the river." Now, I don't know why, what the reason for that was. Then Sefer afterwards said, "Are you crazy?" But Vehbija Karic just shook his head and said, "This is what had taken place in Ahmici, what had happened to us in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the soldier who actually complained about the accommodation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I know that he was a soldier, but I don't know anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was he complaining about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think that they -- these people were sick in their heads. They -- because these civilians there, the local residents, were very accommodating. Or maybe some of those people there had lost a member of their family and were perhaps seeking revenge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So when Karic said those words, who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He was referring to the Croatian civilians, not to the soldiers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And Halilovic made the remark -- could you say again what the remark was so I'm not accused of putting words in your mouth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic said, "Are you in your right mind?" And he made a gesture with his head. And then Vehbija said, "Well, the same thing happened to us in Ahmici." By this he clarified that this order was referring to the Croatian civilians who were there, the elderly civilians, the women, and the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did Sefer Halilovic respond to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As I said, he just made a gesture with his head and said, "Are you in your right mind?" That's all he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did the soldiers have any reaction to this remark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Nobody said anything. They just wondered whether he was in his right mind or not. I found it hard to understand why he had said that. I mean, Vehbija Karic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How did you yourself personally take such a remark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I thought it was a joke. I couldn't take it seriously. Because these were just ordinary civilians. They were not soldiers. This was not combat. And civilians shouldn't be killed if not in combat, not elderly men, and women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: After this meeting, the gentlemen got up and went off in the direction of Jablanica. The soldiers milled about talking until the first twilight, until dusk began to fall. It was about 6.00 when the first murder happened in a house, in the house of Mr. Pero Maric. I was an eyewitness to that. I was sitting there and I saw a man arrive, a soldier. He went into the house and killed Mr. Pero Maric. His wife started screaming, and then he killed his wife too.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who else was in this house when this -- this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Mr. Nihad Vlahovljak was billeted in that house with his fellow fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any others who were present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was his men. They were from another unit. I wasn't familiar with that unit. I didn't know them personally. Just by sight. I can't really recall precisely. All I know is that Nihad Vlahovljak was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were present in that house with Mr. and Mrs. Maric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: About 10 men, 6 to 10 men. We were sitting around having coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this soldier, do you know his name, who came in, the one who shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please: When he walked in, how much time had elapsed before he did the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: About 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So who did he shoot first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First he killed the gentleman, Mr. Pero Maric. And then his wife started screaming. She was ill. She started yelling, "What's going on? What's happening?" He went to the next room, and he killed her as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where was Pero Maric shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where in his house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the wife was shot where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did -- what was the soldier's reaction -- soldiers' reaction, who were in the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When this soldier left the house with his automatic rifle, Nihad said, "What's going on? Are you crazy?" And he said something like, "Don't say anything or I might kill you too."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Nothing. I kept quiet. The man was a fool. He wasn't in his right mind. He must have been crazy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did he leave straight after the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, after the -- what they said, he turned round and left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I stayed there for another few minutes and then I returned to the house where I was accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did you do at this house and what time was it when you went back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, it was twilight, about 7.00. And from there, I went to where Sulejman Lujinovic was. We sat and talked for a while, commenting on all these events. And then I went home -- or rather, to the house in which I was billeted, and I went to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On the next day, when I got up, it was in the morning, 8.00 or 9.00. I'm not sure. And I saw next to the road there were corpses and there was blood. All night this crime had been going on, these murders, which no one was able to prevent -- or rather, nobody paid attention. All those commanders who had been there had done nothing to prevent that crime from happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know who committed the crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I know. It was the soldiers and two men confessed and have been tried in Sarajevo. They were put on trial for four murders. I don't know how many civilians were killed altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which soldiers committed these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Mustafa Hota and this other gentleman, whom I don't know. I don't know his name even.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Any other soldiers that you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you said you saw dead bodies lying around. Can you tell us how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Across from my house, between the house where I slept and the Independent 2nd Battalion, there was one corpse and there were traces of blood along the path, along the right bank of the Neretva. That's where the corpses were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Nothing. I don't know what I could have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did something else happen that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On that day, the last murder took place. We were sitting there. And at about 3.00 p.m. the last murder happened, when Mr. Zulfikar Alispago, also known as Zuka, the commander of the unit in Jablanica, arrived with his men and set up a checkpoint in front of the houses. He put up two checkpoints: One at the entry to Grabovica and the other one at the exit. And he said that no one was to leave Grabovica, no soldier, without his approval. And he collected all those corpses that were by the roadside, put them on a truck, and drove them off somewhere. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What time did Zuka come with his men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Maybe it was around 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how many men did he come with and how did he come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He came by truck. It was some sort of truck. Not a very big one. And there were two soldiers manning each checkpoint. There were his men guarding those checkpoints so that no one could leave Grabovica and no one could find out about the crime. He collected all the corpses and drove them off somewhere. How many men exactly Zuka had with him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did anybody else come that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic came with two children. After Zuka, he brought two children along. Their parents had been killed, their mother, father, grandmother, grandfather, and little sister. And they were found on the road to Jablanica. Delalic Ramiz brought them with him to Grabovica. He lined up all the men from our unit, took out his pistol from its sheathe, and told the children to identify the persons who had murdered their parents. And he said that he would shoot the soldier who had committed the crime if the children identified him. But there were some soldiers absent from the line-up. There were several men who weren't there. The children went from soldier to soldier, looked into their eyes, and in the end they did not identify the perpetrators, the murderers of their parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did Celo arrive before Zuka or after Zuka? Who came first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Celo arrived after Zuka.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were there any bodies in Grabovica at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. Zuka collected all the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps there may have been something along the bank of the Neretva. I don't know how many civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how many bodies did you yourself personally see on that day? Can you just give me a sense of numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Five or six.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what happened to these checkpoints after Zuka's men had taken the bodies? Did they remain or were they taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That night we set out into action, and the checkpoints in Grabovica remained at the entry and exit. It wasn't on the M17, the main road, but on the side road leading to Grabovica. These checkpoints remained, and that night we went into action and we didn't go back to Grabovica any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Tell me, how many soldiers were lined up by Celo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Our unit, the entire brigade. I think 50 or 60 of us from the whole brigade set out, and maybe there were 45 of us. Some people were missing. I can't be precise, but some were absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When you say "brigade," can you tell me, which brigade, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I mean the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you in this line-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You stated to the Court that there was no one identified by these two young boys. Do you know the reason why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, because the perpetrators weren't there, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know that yourself, that the perpetrators were not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Because the children didn't identify them, which means that they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you yourself know that the perpetrators weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: After that, Celo put the children in a car, and with Erdin Arnautovic he drove off to Jablanica, where the children were taken. And what happened to them afterwards, I don't know. All that I know is that they're still alive. If someone from our unit headed by Ramiz Delalic, or Celo, wanted to do this, we would have killed those two children on the spot. Ramiz Delalic certainly saved those children's lives. Because I'm sure there are witnesses who will come to testify here and who will say that there was an order that these two children be killed. I'm not going to talk about it, but this witness will certainly tell you that. He's a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But what about you personally? Did you stay on in Grabovica, or did you leave at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We stayed in Grabovica for another two hours or so. Celo came back after that. The unit was lined up. And at first dusk we set out towards the village of Dreznica. We had to go under cover of darkness because on the M17 there was firing from some elevation. I don't know. So we had to go under cover of night, and we went to the village of Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then after that, you -- you went -- where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We went to Dreznica. We stayed there until 10.00. And then there was an attack on an elevation which was called Antena, I think, in the direction of the village of Vrdi or something like that, in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you ever questioned about these Grabovica murders at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On my return from Herzegovina to Sarajevo - this was about a month or a month and a half later - we were attacked. There was an operation called Trebevic, and Mr. Sefer Halilovic was also put under house arrest. On the 26th of October, they arrested us and detained us in the central prison in Sarajevo. I was in the central prison for four and a half or five months, and I was questioned about the crime in Grabovica on only one occasion. During that time, the investigator was Judge Spoljaric. After that, I wasn't asked anything else, until 1998, when I got a call from Mr. Nikolai in the KNT barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back to Sarajevo, if I may. When you were there, what were your duties, in 1993? When you were in Sarajevo, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary private in the brigade. And I went into action. There would be three or four actions a day. An assault here, an assault there. We were all of us fighting to protect our homes. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What were you doing in Sarajevo itself? Did you have any role in Sarajevo around the -- when the siege was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, no role.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was it you and your brigade, or just you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm referring to myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you in the -- around Sarajevo, were you doing -- were some of your tasks there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. It was only in our area of responsibility, on our line from Mrkovic to Poljine. Nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Whose line was it, when you say "our line"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was the area of responsibility of our brigade, the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you aware at any time whether any troops of your brigade were committing any crime there is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As for our brigade, in the entire area of responsibility there were no crimes that I know of, no murders of civilians, no murders of people of different ethnicities in Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me. When we were arrested in 1993, I heard about a place called Kazani, but I know about that only through the media. There were trials of people who committed those crimes and who are still in prison in Sarajevo today.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was the reputation of the 9th Brigade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Can I now take you to May 1998, please. And if you could tell the -- the Court what happened on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not permissible for prior consistent statements or the like to be led. Now, I'm not sure what my learned friend has in mind here, but unless it's something directly relevant and admissible in the hands of the Prosecutor, then I want to make it clear that I'm going to object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't seem hopeful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from the question, I could not see the directions of the Prosecution, so I will allow the Prosecution to go on for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you remember that date? And what were you doing around that time, May 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: This refers to the statement I made to Mr. Nikolai. He was acting on behalf of the ICTY. At least, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Witness. I'm not talking about the statement of Nikolai. I'm telling you: What were you doing around May 1998? If you can answer that first, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In May 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where were you working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely. In May 1998? You mean that I met Mr. Vehbija Karic, who commented on the statement I made and said, "How can you say something like this?"

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened? Can you tell us? Do you remember that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I wasn't working then. I was sitting in a cafe called Park, near a department store. I was there with some friends of mine having coffee, and Mr. Vehbija Karic came along. He approached me and he said, "Aren't you ashamed making statements like that? How can you say something like that?", referring to what he said in Grabovica. He said there might be consequences of some sort. He laughed and turned and left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What statement was he referring to, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The statement, I'm sure, that I gave to the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo in 1993. We made statements in CSB, in some newspapers. The media would come. This newspaper, that newspaper, always asking for statements about Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In your view, all the statements that you've said you've made, including to the press, did you tell the same story?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, you can't have a question like this seeking to confirm. It's a matter for cross-examination to raise previous statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let us clear the answer of this witness. Then you could cross-examine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. As the Court pleases. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, can you tell -- give me the answer. Have they been consistent? Have you told the same story?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I always told the same story. The only discrepancy that turned up was in the statement that Mr. Nikolai took, because he didn't let us read it or anything. He worked on a laptop and he said he was sending it directly to The Hague Tribunal and there was nothing to sign. And there was even no interpreter present, at least very little.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be my examination-in-chief from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think it is time for us to have a break, and we'll resume at 11.00. After that, there will be some cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: (redacted). Witness, I want to put something to you. You're one of the killers, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You were right there when the killing took place; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You had a firearm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You discharged that firearm on a number of occasions during your stay down there in Grabovica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. I fired only during the offensive, in action. Outside Grabovica, in the only operation that took place at the time, that is, the Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: For many years, you told a plainly dishonest story to conceal your proximity to the killings and in particular to the killing of Pero Maric; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In statement after statement, in account after account, you never did admit that you were right there when Pero Maric was shot; is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Answer my question, first of all. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, your client, the then-commander of the Operation Neretva, and also commander of the Operation Trebevic, the distinguished commander had also covered up for the murders for a number of years without saying who the perpetrators were and why these crimes had been committed in order for light to be shed onto these crimes in the past couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The answer to my question is yes, you've lied repeatedly concerning your direct presence at the shooting of Pero Maric; is that true? Or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I didn't lie. This was our order that we weren't supposed to say anything to anyone. You should not have put this question to me but, rather, to the authorities in Sarajevo, who had placed us under arrest on the 26th of October, 1993. And this is the question that you should put to these people to see what the reasons were for the cover-up, why the truth about these events had been covered up for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You always knew in your own mind that you were right at hand when Pero Maric was shot; correct? You always knew that, because that was true; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I always knew that. But we weren't allowed to say anything about it because such were our orders. When we were in the prison, we were told that we were not supposed to say anything further on this matter. We were invoked some articles to the effect that we might incur a life sentence or even a death penalty. This was something that came from the Supreme Command and the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You came -- I'm sorry, in what sense did that come from the court, please, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: From the court. Because we were first interrogated and then all the interrogations were put a stop to. This probably had come from the Supreme Command, from someone who must have been more powerful than the court and whose -- in whose interest it was to cover up the truth to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And just in terms of that cover-up - and I won't spend much time on this now - but you say that was communicated to you after your arrest on the 26th of October, 1993 in the course of Operation Trebevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: This was halfway through the sentence that I was serving. That was those four and a half to five months, when my proceedings were suddenly drawn to a close. And this is something that has been documented in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly. You came to know within the last couple of months that Enes Sakrak was coming here to give evidence that he was present when Pero Maric was shot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And what I put to you is this: You realised then that your lies were going to come unstuck and be revealed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, I'm not lying. I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You knew then that an eyewitness to the shooting of Pero Maric was capable of putting you, (redacted) correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: How do you mean right there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I mean is that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just indicate now that there may need to be some redaction. I've now understood the note that I was given, so my apologies for (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you -- sorry, Witness, what I'm putting to you is this: That you came to know very well that your presence at the shooting of Pero Maric was about to come out in this Tribunal. You came to know that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I've said that already. I was not empowered to say anything about that because of the pressure and the threats in Sarajevo. Even today I fear my return into the town because threats have been levelled at me. Even during my stay here in The Hague, I received messages from my relatives and my brother to the effect that there are threats against me. And tomorrow I might not even be alive. You here defend a person who potentially knew of these crimes, murders. And now the question remains as to why he had never launched an investigation into what was happening in Grabovica. I was just a private, a common soldier, and he held the rank of a general in the army. He was then the Chief of the Main Staff, because at the time there still wasn't the function of a commander. Why didn't he himself show up and report these crimes? You are calling upon me, a mortal, a private, that I should have done something whilst it was not in my power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, don't -- don't misunderstand what's being put to you, Mr. Sakrak -- Mr. -- sorry, Mr. -- Witness D. I'm not putting that to you at all. What I'm putting to you is that you're a murderer. Do you understand that that's what's being put to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm not a murderer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And then for the first time when you spoke to the learned Prosecutor here after arriving in The Hague, you revealed the truth or part of the truth, anyway, that you were present at the shooting of Pero Maric and that you did see several bodies in the village. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that here because at the time over there I didn't have the occasion to nor the person whom I was able to reveal this to. Because that's the way the state functioned at the time. If you had money, you were able to do whatever you wanted; if you didn't, you couldn't. All these events could have been brought to light in Sarajevo earlier on without having it to come to this stage where we have to tell the story in front of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor here that you've received threats even since you've been in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When did you tell -- which Prosecutor did you tell that to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I've told that to the gentleman in charge of security for witnesses here. I don't know what their title is. I told them so, and they were there when I was called to answer a phone call. And then a security person came here, a person in charge of security. I don't know his name. And I spoke to him yesterday in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you've continued to allege, I take it, that threats are being made to your family; is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you go to the police in Sarajevo about these threats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had no reason to. In view of what the situation with the police is, it doesn't really make any difference whether you report something like that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And what I put to you is that you will blame anyone else and shift the blame onto anyone else in the hope that your own guilt is never revealed. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Had I been guilty of committing a crime or anything in that sense in relation to Grabovica, I would admit that now I -- and say that I committed this -- or, rather, crime to relieve myself of the burden, and I believe that any person who has conscience would do something like that, because a person committing such an act must be sick in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So who are the people who committed these crimes, (redacted) What are their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Didn't you say to Ms. Chana here in the course of proofing the following: "I have myself talked to these soldiers who did kill and asked how they could do this. They all talked about it as if they had spilt a glass of water. No remorse was displayed. I can't tell the names of these soldiers, as I am frightened of the consequences." Now, that's what you told Ms. Chana just a couple of days ago, isn't it, that you knew -- that you couldn't tell their names because you're frightened of the consequences? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Don't worry about the consequences. Tell us the names, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would ask that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You mentioned -- I'll just repeat the question because we're now back in the open session. You mentioned earlier on a person in Sarajevo who had a document in their possession, an order, which they were going to bring to court here. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He is in possession of an order in relation to the Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: All the commanders of the brigades involved are in possession of the order that they had received from Sefer Halilovic. All of the commanders of the units involved in the Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who is the person you referred to in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic is one of those who has the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you know that Ramiz Delalic is coming to give evidence here with that order because you've been speaking about these proceedings with him, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, we didn't talk, but I know given the proceedings so far that he is going to be called here as a witness and bring all the documents he has with him. He even has a tape, a recording, that originated from some people who asked of me to change my statement to say that Sefer Halilovic was not a commander of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: How do you know he's got such a tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
